title: What are Compact Object Headers?
keyPoints: Every Java object has a header: mark word (8 bytes) + class pointer (4 bytes compressed) = 12 bytes minimum
Project Lilliput aims to reduce headers to 8 bytes (combine mark word + class pointer)
Small objects (boolean, byte) can be >50% header overhead
Reducing header size saves significant memory for applications with many small objects
Expected in future Java releases (experimental in JDK 23+)

s1_definition.oneliner: Every Java object has a 12-byte header (mark word + class pointer). Project Lilliput aims to reduce this to 8 bytes, saving memory for applications with many small objects.
s1_definition.profdef:
Object header layout (HotSpot 64-bit, compressed oops):

- **Mark word:** 8 bytes – hash code, GC age, lock state.
- **Class pointer:** 4 bytes (compressed) – points to the class metadata.
- **Total:** 12 bytes minimum header before any fields.
- **Alignment:** Objects padded to 8-byte boundary.
s1_definition.analogy: Every bank account file has a cover sheet (header) with metadata (account type, creation date, lock status). Even a file with just one page of data still needs the full cover sheet. Compact headers use a smaller cover sheet.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Current: Mark (8) + Class Ptr (4) = 12 bytes header
  Lilliput: Mark + Class combined = 8 bytes header
  Valhalla: Value types = 0 bytes header (inline)

  Boolean object: 16 bytes total, 1 byte data → 94% overhead
  → Compact headers save significant memory at scale
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Every Java object has a 12-byte header (mark word + class pointer). For small objects, this is the majority of the memory. Project Lilliput aims to reduce headers to 8 bytes. Use JOL to inspect your objects' actual memory layout.

One sentence to remember: object headers are 12 bytes minimum – Project Lilliput shrinks them to 8 bytes for memory savings at scale.
